articles.title: How to Convert a Normal Switch to a Smart Switch
articles.excerpt: You can convert a normal switch to a smart switch without replacing the switchboard. Here is how a retrofit module does it, step by step.
articles.body_html:
Many people type "convert normal switch to smart switch" into Google and expect the answer to be a new glass touch panel. It does not have to be. In most Indian homes the switch on the wall can stay exactly where it is. A small module goes behind it, inside the switchbox, and the same switch starts working from your phone as well.

This guide explains what happens inside the box, what your home needs for it, and where this method is not the right answer.

What "smart" means for a switch

A normal switch does one thing: it joins or breaks the circuit when you press it. A smart switch does the same job, and it can also be told to do it from somewhere else, such as an app or a schedule. Nothing about the light or the fan changes. Only the way the command reaches it changes.

There are two ways to get there. You can replace the whole switch plate with a smart one, or you can keep the plate and add the smart part behind it. The second way is called retrofit, and it is what Homeasy does.

How to convert normal switch to smart switch with a retrofit module

The work is done by a trained electrician. In simple steps:

  1. Power off. The supply to that switchboard is switched off at the distribution board.

  2. Open the plate. The switch plate is unscrewed and eased forward. The wires stay connected to the house.

  3. Fit the module. A compact module is connected between your existing switch and the wire going to the light, fan or appliance. It sits inside the switchbox, behind the switches.

  4. Close and test. The plate goes back on. The switch is tested by hand first, then from the app.

From the outside, the switchboard looks the same as it did in the morning. You can read the full process on our how it works page.

What your home needs

Retrofit is simple when three things are in place. Our free home survey checks each of them before any work is quoted.

  • Space in the switchbox. The module needs a little room behind the switches. Many boxes have it. Very shallow or overcrowded boxes may not.

  • The right wires. Some modules need a neutral wire in the box. Many homes have one, and some older homes do not. We check every box. A no-neutral module is planned, and it is not available yet.

  • Wi-Fi at home. Control from the app needs Wi-Fi and internet. Your switches keep working by hand even when the internet is down.

Which module does what

Different loads need different modules. A light and a geyser should never be treated the same way.

  • Lights and small appliances: a smart relay module.

  • Ceiling fans: a fan controller, so you can change speed and not only switch on and off.

  • Geyser, AC and water motor: a power module built for heavy loads.

  • AC and TV with a remote: an IR remote module that sends the same signals as the handset.

The products page lists each one and what it controls.

When retrofit is not the right answer

We would rather tell you plainly than promise that it fits every home. Retrofit may not suit a switchbox that has no space left, wiring that is damaged or unsafe, or a board that needs repair anyway. In those cases the survey report says so, and any fix is agreed with you before you pay for anything.

Should you do it yourself?

Modules are sold online, and the wiring looks simple in a video. In a real switchbox it is easy to mix up the live and load wires, overload a small module with a heavy appliance, or leave a loose joint behind the plate. Mains wiring is not a place to learn by trial. Use a trained electrician, and ask who you can call if something stops working later.

What it is like afterwards

Day to day, nothing is taken away. Guests and parents use the switches as they always have. You get a few extra things: switching off a light from bed, checking from the office whether the geyser was left on, and setting a schedule for the things you forget.

If you want to convert normal switch to smart switch in your own home, the first step is a look inside your switchboxes. You can book a free home survey, and we will tell you what is possible in each room. Our public launch is planned for January 2027, and until then homes can join early access.

articles.title: Smart Switch vs Normal Switch: What Really Changes
articles.excerpt: Smart switch vs normal switch: what is different in daily use, in wiring and in upkeep, and how a retrofit module gives you both in one.
articles.body_html:
The question "smart switch vs normal switch" sounds like a choice between two products. In practice it is a choice about how you want to control the same light, fan or geyser. This article compares the two honestly, including the points where a normal switch is still the better tool.

What each one does

A normal switch is a simple mechanical part. Press it and the circuit closes. Press it again and it opens. It needs no power of its own, no network and no app, and it lasts for years.

A smart switch can do that same job, and it can also be operated without touching it: from an app, on a schedule, or as part of a scene such as "Good night" that turns several things off together. To do this it contains electronics, and it needs a connection to your home network.

Smart switch vs normal switch in daily life

  • Walking into a room. A normal switch wins. Nothing is faster than your hand. This is why a good smart setup keeps the physical switch working.

  • Leaving the house. Smart wins. You can check and switch off what was left on, instead of going back upstairs or worrying on the way to work.

  • Things on a timetable. Smart wins. A geyser that switches itself off, or a porch light that follows a schedule, removes a small daily chore.

  • Guests, children and elders. A normal switch wins, because everybody already knows how to use it.

  • When the internet is down. A normal switch is unaffected. A smart one should still work by hand; only the app control pauses.

What changes behind the wall

There are two kinds of smart switch, and they are very different to install.

Replacement panels take the place of your whole switch plate, often with touch buttons. They look new, and they also mean a new look for the room, a learning curve for the family, and sometimes changes to the box in the wall.

Retrofit modules sit inside the existing switchbox, behind the switches you already have. The plate stays. The switch keeps working by hand, and the module adds control from the app. This is the method Homeasy uses, and you can see it explained on the how it works page.

What a smart switch needs that a normal one does not

  • Wi-Fi and internet for app control.

  • Suitable wiring. Some modules need a neutral wire in the switchbox. A survey checks this box by box.

  • The right module for the load. A light, a fan and a geyser need different modules. Putting a heavy appliance on a small module is unsafe.

  • Someone to call. Electronics can fail in a way a plain switch does not. Ask about warranty and support before you buy. Homeasy modules carry a 3-year warranty against manufacturing defects.

Where a normal switch is still enough

Not every point in a home needs to be smart. A storeroom light, a rarely used socket or a bathroom exhaust is often fine as it is. Most families start with the things they forget or cannot reach easily: the geyser, bedroom lights and fans, the AC and outdoor lights. You can add more rooms later.

Do you have to choose?

With retrofit you do not. The honest summary of smart switch vs normal switch is that each is better at different moments, and a module behind your existing switch gives you both: the hand switch for the moments when you are in the room, and the app for when you are not.

Voice control with Alexa or Google is a common reason people look at smart switches. For Homeasy it is planned and not available yet, and we will say so until it is ready. The FAQ covers this and other common questions.

How to decide for your home

Walk through your day and note the switches you wish you could reach from somewhere else. That list is your starting point. Then have the switchboxes checked, because the wiring decides what is possible. A free home survey does exactly that, and you get a plain answer for each room before any money changes hands.
articles.cover_alt: A hand pressing a normal wall switch beside a phone showing the same light in an app

articles.title: Smart Home Without Internet: What Works and What Doesn't
articles.excerpt: Can you run a smart home without internet? Your switches still work by hand. Here is what stops, what keeps working, and how to plan for it.
articles.body_html:
Internet connections drop. Routers hang, recharges lapse and lines get cut during road work. So it is fair to ask what a smart home without internet actually does. The short answer for a retrofit home: every switch keeps working by hand, and the app waits until the connection is back.

This article goes through it piece by piece, without pretending the internet does not matter.

Three different things people call "internet"

It helps to separate three things that often get mixed up.

  • Electricity. If the power is off, nothing electrical runs, smart or not.

  • Wi-Fi. This is the local network made by your router inside the house.

  • Internet. This is the line from your router to the outside world.

Your Wi-Fi can be working while the internet is down. Both matter for app control, in different ways.

What keeps working in a smart home without internet

In a home fitted with Homeasy modules, the switches on your wall always work by hand. This is the main reason we retrofit behind the existing switch instead of replacing it with a screen or a touch panel. If the router is off, the recharge has run out, or the family member with the app is travelling, everyone at home can still switch a light or a fan on and off the normal way.

Nothing needs to be "reset" for this. The physical switch is part of the circuit, as it was before.

What stops until the connection returns

We say this plainly on our site: app control needs Wi-Fi and internet. While the connection is down, you cannot switch things from your phone, and you cannot check from outside whether something was left on.

If you see a product claiming that everything works with no network at all, ask exactly which features are meant. Being clear about this before you buy saves disappointment later.

How to make outages matter less

A few simple habits make the difference between a small pause and a real nuisance.

  1. Place the router well. Smart modules sit inside metal switchboxes, and walls weaken the signal. A router in a central spot serves the far rooms better than one hidden in a corner cupboard.

  2. Keep the router powered. In many homes the router goes off with every power cut. Keeping it on backup power, where you have it, keeps the network steady.

  3. Use a reliable plan. App control does not need a fast connection. It needs one that stays up.

  4. Keep the switches reachable. Do not block switchboards with furniture on the assumption that the phone will do everything.

What about power cuts?

A power cut is a different event from an internet outage. When the mains supply is off, the appliance has no power, so there is nothing to control. When the supply returns, your switches work by hand as usual. How a home behaves on inverter backup depends on its wiring, and it is one of the things we look at during the survey.

Is a smart home worth it if my internet is unreliable?

It can be, as long as your expectations match what you are buying. If your connection is down for hours every day, you will use the app less, and the hand switches more. You lose nothing you had before. If your connection is mostly fine with the occasional drop, a retrofit setup suits you well, because the fallback is the switch you have always used.

Where the idea of a smart home without internet goes wrong is with setups that remove the normal switch. Then a network problem becomes a "we cannot turn on the light" problem. Keep the physical switch, and the worst case is simply an ordinary home for a while.

Questions to ask before you buy

  • Do my existing switches keep working by hand?

  • What exactly needs Wi-Fi, and what needs internet?

  • What happens after a power cut?

  • Who do I call if a module stops responding?

You will find our answers in the FAQ and on the app page. To see what suits your home, book a free home survey, and we will check the switchboxes and the Wi-Fi reach room by room.
articles.cover_alt: Family member switching on a light by hand while the Wi-Fi router shows no connection

articles.title: Home Automation Cost in India: What Decides Your Quote
articles.excerpt: Home automation cost in India depends on a few clear things: points, loads, wiring and the method used. Here is how a quote is built.
articles.body_html:
Search for "home automation cost in india" and you will find figures that differ by ten times or more. They are not all wrong. They are describing very different jobs, from a single smart plug to a full rewired villa. This article does not give you a number, because an honest number needs a look at your home. It explains what makes a quote go up or down, so you can read any quote with confidence.

Why one price does not fit every home

Two flats with the same number of rooms can need very different work. One has deep switchboxes with neat wiring. The other has shallow boxes, old joints and no neutral wire in half the rooms. The first is a simple retrofit. The second needs more time and perhaps some repair. A fixed price that ignores this is either padded for the worst case or will change later.

The five things that decide home automation cost in India

  1. How many points you make smart. A "point" is one thing you control: a light, a fan, a geyser. More points mean more modules and more fitting time. You do not have to do the whole house at once.

  2. What kind of loads they are. A light needs a small relay. A fan needs a controller that handles speed. A geyser, AC or water motor needs a module built for heavy loads. These are different parts with different prices.

  3. The method. Retrofit modules go behind your existing switches, so the switchboards, wall finish and wiring stay. Replacing boards with new touch panels, or rewiring for a wired system, adds material, labour and repair work on walls.

  4. The state of your wiring. If a box needs a fix before a module can go in safely, that is extra work. A proper survey finds this before the quote, not after.

  5. What is included. Installation, app setup, taxes, warranty and support may or may not be in the headline figure. Ask.

What a good quote should show

Whoever you buy from, a quote you can trust has these things written down:

  • A room-by-room list of what will be made smart, and with which module.

  • Anything that cannot be done, and why.

  • Any wiring fix that is needed, stated before you pay.

  • The full amount including taxes.

  • The warranty period and who to contact for support.

At Homeasy your exact price is confirmed after the free survey, and the written quote shows the full amount, including taxes, before you decide. Homeasy modules carry a 3-year warranty against manufacturing defects. Our pricing page explains the packages.

Ways to keep the cost sensible

  • Start with what you will use. The geyser, bedroom lights and fans, the AC and outdoor lights are the usual first choices. A storeroom bulb can wait.

  • Keep your switchboards. If you like how they look and they are in good condition, retrofit avoids paying for new plates and wall repair.

  • Plan in stages. Do the rooms you live in most, then add others later. Adding rooms afterwards is normal.

  • Do not buy on the unit price alone. A cheap module fitted badly, with nobody to call, costs more in the end.

Hidden costs to ask about

Some costs appear only after the work has started. Ask about each one in advance: charges for visits, charges for the app or any subscription, the cost of fixing a wall or a plate if it is damaged, and what happens if a module fails after the warranty. The Homeasy app will be free for every Homeasy customer.

Get a rough idea before the survey

If you want to think it through first, our estimator lets you pick your rooms and appliances and shows which modules you would need. It is a planning tool and not a quote.

The honest way to get your number

The only reliable answer to the question of home automation cost in india for your home is a survey followed by a written quote. Ours is free across Bihar. Book a free home survey, and we will check every switchbox and tell you plainly what is possible and what it will cost.

articles.title: WiFi Smart Switch for Home: How It Works and What It Needs
articles.excerpt: Thinking about a wifi smart switch for home? Here is how it connects, what your router and wiring need, and what to check before you buy.
articles.body_html:
A wifi smart switch for home use is the simplest way most families meet home automation. There is no separate control box to buy and no new wiring through the walls. The switch, or a module behind it, talks to the router you already have. This guide explains how that works and what to check before you choose one.

How a Wi-Fi smart switch works

Inside the switch or module there is a small relay and a Wi-Fi radio. The relay does the switching, the same job your finger does on a normal switch. The radio connects to your home router. When you tap a button in the app, the command travels over the internet to your router, then over Wi-Fi to the module, and the relay switches the light or fan.

That is why app control needs both Wi-Fi and internet. It is also why a well-designed setup keeps the wall switch working by hand, so a network problem never stops you from switching on a light.

Two forms of wifi smart switch for home

A replacement switch or touch panel. The old plate comes off and a new smart plate goes on. The room gets a new look, and the family has to learn the new panel.

A retrofit module. A compact module is fitted inside the existing switchbox, behind the switches you already have. From the outside nothing changes. This is the approach Homeasy takes, and the how it works page shows it step by step.

What your Wi-Fi needs

  • Signal in every room that has a module. Modules sit inside metal boxes in the wall, which weakens the signal. If your phone struggles for signal near a switchboard, a module there will struggle too.

  • A router in a sensible place. Central and in the open is better than inside a cupboard at one end of the house.

  • A steady connection. Speed matters very little. Staying connected matters a lot.

Ask your installer which Wi-Fi settings the modules need. It is a small detail that is much easier to sort out before installation day than after.

What your wiring needs

Wi-Fi is only half of it. The switchbox has to suit the module.

  • Space. There must be room behind the switches for the module.

  • A neutral wire, for some modules. Not every Indian switchbox has one. A survey checks each box.

  • A module that matches the load. Lights, fans and heavy appliances such as geysers each need a different module.

Our products page lists the modules for lights, fans, heavy loads and remote-controlled ACs and TVs.

What you can do with it

  • Switch things on and off from the app, at home or away.

  • Group devices into rooms and scenes, such as one tap to switch off the whole bedroom.

  • Set schedules, for example a geyser that turns off by itself.

  • Share control with your family.

Voice control through Alexa or Google is something many people ask about. For Homeasy it is planned and not available yet.

Common mistakes when buying

  1. Buying before checking the box. A module that does not fit, or needs a wire you do not have, is money wasted.

  2. Using one type of module for everything. A small relay is not made for a geyser.

  3. Ignoring the Wi-Fi reach. Check the far rooms first.

  4. Losing the hand switch. Make sure the wall switch still works when the network does not.

  5. No support. Ask about the warranty and who comes if a module fails.

Is your data a concern?

It is reasonable to ask what an app knows about your home. Read the privacy policy of whichever product you choose, use a strong Wi-Fi password, and share app access only with people who live with you.

Where to start

Choosing a wifi smart switch for home is less about brands and more about your own switchboxes and router. Start with a check of both. Our free home survey covers the wiring in each box and the Wi-Fi reach in each room, and you get a plain list of what will work.

articles.title: Smart Fan Regulator: Control Fan Speed From Your Phone
articles.excerpt: A smart fan regulator lets you change ceiling fan speed from your phone while the wall regulator stays. Here is how it works and what to check.
articles.body_html:
The ceiling fan runs more hours than anything else in an Indian home, and it is the one thing people most want to adjust without getting out of bed. A smart fan regulator makes that possible. This guide explains how it differs from a simple smart switch, and what has to be checked in your switchbox first.

Why a fan needs more than an on/off module

A light is either on or off. A fan has speeds. If you put a plain on/off relay on a fan, you can start and stop it from the app, and the speed stays wherever the wall regulator was left. That is half the job.

A fan also behaves differently from a light electrically, because it has a motor. A module made for lights is not the right part for it. Fans need a controller designed for fans.

How a smart fan regulator works

A fan controller module is fitted inside the switchbox, on the fan's circuit. It takes over the job of setting the speed, in steps, and it accepts commands from the app. You choose the speed on your phone, and the module sets it.

The Homeasy Fan Controller gives you fan on/off and speed from the app. Because homes have different kinds of regulators, we confirm the fit with your regulator at the survey instead of assuming it.

Regulators found in Indian homes

  • Old box-type regulators. Large, warm to the touch, with a rotary knob. They take up a lot of space in the board.

  • Electronic step regulators. The compact modular type with a knob that clicks through speeds. These are the most common in newer boards.

  • Fans with their own remote. Some newer fans have the speed control inside the fan and come with a handset.

Each of these calls for a slightly different approach, which is why the survey looks at the regulator and the fan, not only at the switch.

What is checked before fitting

  1. Space in the box. The controller needs room behind the plate.

  2. The wiring in that box. Including whether a neutral wire is present, where the module needs one.

  3. The type of fan and regulator. To confirm the controller suits it.

  4. Wi-Fi reach at that board. App control needs Wi-Fi and internet.

What you can do once it is fitted

  • Change the speed from bed, or switch the fan off in a room you have left.

  • Include the fan in a scene, so "Good night" can lower the speed and switch off the lights together.

  • Set a schedule, such as a lower speed in the early hours when it gets cooler.

  • Let family members use the same controls from their own phones.

Common questions

Will the fan make a humming noise? Hum can come from a controller that does not suit the fan. Matching the two properly is the reason we check at the survey.

Can I still use the fan without the phone? Yes. Your switches work by hand as before, even if the internet is down.

Does it work with Alexa or Google? People often search for a smart fan regulator with voice control. For Homeasy, voice assistant support is planned and not available yet.

Do I need a new fan? No. The point of retrofit is to keep the fan and the switchboard you have.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Fitting a light relay on a fan circuit.

  • Buying a controller before anyone has opened the switchbox.

  • Leaving both an old regulator and a new controller trying to set the speed on the same fan.

  • Skipping the Wi-Fi check in the bedroom farthest from the router.

Getting it done

A fan is a small upgrade that you notice every single night. If you want it done properly, have the regulator and the box looked at first. The products page describes the Fan Controller, and the installation page explains what happens on the day. When you are ready, book a free home survey and we will check every fan point in your home.

articles.title: Geyser Smart Switch: Schedule Hot Water, Stop the Worry
articles.excerpt: A geyser smart switch lets you schedule hot water and switch the geyser off from anywhere. Here is what it needs and why the module matters.
articles.body_html:
"Did anyone switch off the geyser?" is asked in almost every Indian home, usually from the car. A geyser smart switch answers it. You can check from your phone, switch it off from anywhere, and set a schedule so it is not left on by mistake. This guide covers how it works and why a geyser must never be treated like a light.

Why the geyser is different

A geyser is a heavy load. It draws far more current than a light or a fan, which is why it sits on a larger, higher-rated switch and socket. Any smart module on that circuit has to be built for the same heavy load.

This is the most important point in this article: a small relay module made for lights must not be used on a geyser. It can overheat. If a seller offers one module "for everything", ask what its rating is and what it is meant for.

How a geyser smart switch works

A module rated for heavy loads is fitted inside the switchbox of the geyser point, behind the existing switch. The switch on the wall keeps working by hand. The module adds two things: control from the app, and schedules.

The Homeasy Power Module (16A) is the one we use for geysers, ACs and water motors. As with every module, the box is checked at the survey before anything is promised.

What you can do with it

  • Schedule the morning. Have hot water ready when you wake up, and have the geyser switch itself off afterwards.

  • Switch off from anywhere. If you left in a hurry, open the app and turn it off.

  • Check the state. See whether it is on without walking to the bathroom.

  • Share it. Everyone at home can use the same schedule and controls.

App control needs Wi-Fi and internet. The wall switch works by hand whether or not the internet is up.

Does it save electricity?

We do not quote a savings percentage, because we have no measurements of our own to stand behind one, and every home is different. What can be said plainly is this: a geyser that is left on for hours after the last bath is using power for nothing, and a schedule or a quick tap in the app stops that. How much it matters in your home depends on how often it happens.

What is checked at the survey

  1. The geyser point and its switch. Its rating and condition.

  2. The wiring. Loose or heat-damaged joints at a geyser point are fixed before a module goes in, and you are told first.

  3. Space in the box. The power module needs room.

  4. Wi-Fi at the bathroom wall. Bathrooms are often the weakest spot for signal.

Safety comes first

A smart module does not replace the safety parts of your geyser or your home. The thermostat and safety valve inside the geyser, proper earthing, and the protective devices in your distribution board all stay exactly as important as before. A schedule is a convenience. It is not a safety device.

For the same reason, this is not a do-it-yourself job. Heavy-load wiring should be handled by a trained electrician who follows a safety checklist. You can read ours on the installation page.

Common questions

Will my existing switch still work? Yes. It works by hand exactly as before.

What if the internet is down in the morning? Use the wall switch. App control returns when the connection does.

Can the same module run my water motor or AC? The Power Module is built for those heavy loads as well. Each point is checked on its own.

What about warranty? Homeasy modules carry a 3-year warranty against manufacturing defects.

Where to begin

For many families the geyser is the first thing worth making smart, because it is the one that causes the most second-guessing. Choosing a geyser smart switch is mostly about using the correct heavy-load module and fitting it safely. See the module on the products page, or book a free home survey and we will check your geyser point along with the rest of the house.

articles.title: How to Control AC From Phone With an IR Remote Module
articles.excerpt: You can control AC from phone even if the AC is not a smart model. Here is how an IR remote module does it, and what to check in your room.
articles.body_html:
Most air conditioners in Indian homes are ordinary remote-controlled units, not "smart" models. You can still control AC from phone with them. The trick is a small module that speaks the same language as the handset in your drawer. This guide explains how it works, where it should be placed, and what it cannot do.

Two ways an AC can be controlled

There are two separate things you might want to control.

  • The power to the AC. This is the heavy switch on the wall. Making it smart lets you cut or restore power to the unit.

  • The AC's own settings. On and off, temperature, mode and fan speed. These are normally set with the remote.

Cutting the power is not the same as setting the temperature, and an AC should normally be switched off with its remote first. So for everyday use, the second kind of control is the one that matters.

How to control AC from phone using infrared

Your AC remote sends commands as pulses of infrared light, which is invisible to the eye. An IR remote module can send the same pulses. Once it is set up for your AC, you tap a button in the app, the module sends the signal, and the AC responds as if you had pressed the handset.

The Homeasy IR Remote works with most remote-controlled ACs and TVs. Brands and models differ, so we check yours at the survey instead of promising that it works with everything.

Placement matters

Infrared travels in straight lines and does not pass through walls. The module must be able to "see" the front of the AC, where the receiver is. In practice that means:

  • The module is placed in the same room as the AC.

  • Nothing solid sits between the two, such as a cupboard or a pillar.

  • One module serves one room. A TV in the same room can often be covered by the same module if it can see both.

What you can do with it

  • Switch the AC on before you reach home, so the room is comfortable when you walk in.

  • Switch it off after you have left, when you realise it is still running.

  • Set the temperature without hunting for the remote.

  • Use a schedule, for example to turn the AC off in the early morning.

  • Add it to a scene, so "Good night" sets the AC, lowers the fan and turns off the lights together.

App control needs Wi-Fi and internet. Your handset keeps working as usual, so nobody at home has to change how they use the AC.

What it does not do

It is better to know the limits before you buy.

  • Infrared is one-way. If someone changes the AC with the handset, the app may not show the new setting.

  • It does not make the AC use less power by itself. It only makes it easier to switch off when it is not needed.

  • It cannot control an AC that has no working remote receiver.

  • Voice control through Alexa or Google is planned for Homeasy and is not available yet.

What about the heavy switch on the wall?

The AC's power point can be made smart too, with a module built for heavy loads, the same family used for geysers and water motors. Whether you need that as well depends on how you use the AC. Many homes are happy with the IR module alone.

What is checked at the survey

  1. The make and model of the AC, and whether its remote signals are supported.

  2. A good spot for the module with a clear view of the AC.

  3. Wi-Fi reach in that room.

  4. The AC's power point, if you want that controlled as well.

Getting started

If you want to control AC from phone without replacing the AC, an IR module is the simple route. The products page describes the IR Remote and the Power Module, and the app page shows how rooms, scenes and schedules work. To check your own AC, book a free home survey.

articles.excerpt: Planning home automation in Patna? Here is what suits local homes, what a survey checks, and the questions to ask any company before you pay.
articles.body_html:
Interest in home automation in Patna has grown quickly, and so has the confusion. Showrooms display glass touch panels, online shops sell loose modules, and electricians each have their own opinion. This guide is for a homeowner in Patna or elsewhere in Bihar who wants a clear, practical way to think about it.

What homes here are usually like

A large share of homes in Patna are already built and lived in: family houses that have grown floor by floor, and flats that were finished years ago. The switchboards are in the wall, the paint is done, and nobody wants to break tiles or chase new wiring through plaster.

That is the starting point for any sensible plan. The question is not "what is the most advanced system?" It is "what can be added to this house without tearing it up?"

Retrofit: home automation in Patna without rewiring

Retrofit means fitting a compact module inside the existing switchbox, behind the switches you already have. The plates stay. The walls stay. The switches keep working by hand, and you also get control from an app.

This is what Homeasy does, and it is why we call ourselves retrofit-first. You can see the method on the how it works page. It suits lived-in homes because the work is done box by box, room by room, without a renovation.

What can be made smart

  • Lights and small appliances, with a smart relay.

  • Ceiling fans, including speed, with a fan controller.

  • Geyser, AC and water motor, with a module built for heavy loads.

  • Remote-controlled ACs and TVs, with an IR remote module.

Most families begin with the geyser, the bedrooms and the outdoor lights, then add other rooms later.

What a home survey checks

No two houses are wired the same way, so the first step is always a visit. A proper survey looks at:

  1. Each switchbox: the space inside it and the condition of the wiring.

  2. Whether a neutral wire is present in the box, which some modules need.

  3. The loads on each switch, so the right module is chosen.

  4. Wi-Fi reach in each room, since app control needs Wi-Fi and internet.

  5. Anything that should be repaired first, which you are told about before you pay.

Our survey is free, and we survey homes across Bihar. Our head office and pilot are in Patna. The installation page explains survey day and installation day.

Questions to ask any company

  • Will my existing switches still work by hand?

  • Does my switchboard look different afterwards?

  • Who does the installation, and are they trained for this work?

  • Is the price written down in full, including taxes, before I decide?

  • What is the warranty, and who comes if something fails?

  • Is the company local, and can I reach a person on the phone?

A company that answers these plainly is worth your time. One that avoids them is not, whatever the brochure says.

Things to be careful about

  • Big claims. "Works with every switchboard" and fixed savings percentages are easy to print and hard to prove.

  • Loose modules fitted by anyone. A heavy appliance on the wrong module is a safety risk.

  • No written quote. If it is not written, it will change.

  • Features that are "coming". Ask what works today. For Homeasy, voice control with Alexa and Google is planned and not available yet, and we say so.

Where Homeasy stands today

Homeasy Automation is a Patna company, incorporated in 2025. Our public launch is planned for January 2027. Until then we are inviting pilot homes in Patna to join early access, and everyone on the list gets a special early-access offer that is confirmed in a written quote before any payment.

The first step

Good home automation in Patna starts with a look inside your own switchboxes, not with a catalogue. Book a free home survey, and we will tell you plainly what is possible in each room. If you would like to talk first, the contact page has our phone, WhatsApp and email.

articles.title: Home Automation for Beginners: Where to Start at Home
articles.excerpt: Home automation for beginners, in plain words: what it is, what to make smart first, what your home needs, and the mistakes worth avoiding.
articles.body_html:
If the words relay, module and scene mean nothing to you yet, this is the right page. It is a guide to home automation for beginners, written for an ordinary Indian home and with no jargon left unexplained. By the end you will know what the idea is, what to start with, and what to ask before spending anything.

What home automation actually is

Home automation means being able to control the electrical things in your home in more ways than by walking to the switch. You can switch them from a phone, have them follow a timetable, or change several together with one tap.

That is all it is. The light is the same light. The fan is the same fan. Only the control is new.

The four words you will hear

  • Module. A small electronic part that makes one switch smart. It can sit inside the switchbox, behind your existing switch.

  • App. The program on your phone where you see and control your rooms.

  • Scene. One button that does several things together, such as "Good night" switching off the lights and lowering the fan.

  • Schedule. A timetable, such as the geyser switching off at a set time every morning.

Home automation for beginners: what to make smart first

You do not need to do the whole house. Start with the things that bother you most. For most families these are:

  1. The geyser. So it is never left on by mistake.

  2. Bedroom lights and fans. So you can change them from bed.

  3. The AC. So you can switch it on before you arrive, or off after you have left.

  4. Outdoor and staircase lights. So they follow a timetable and nobody has to remember.

Everything else can wait. Adding more rooms later is normal.

Do you have to change your switchboards?

No. This surprises most beginners. There are two methods. One replaces your switch plates with new smart panels. The other, called retrofit, keeps your plates and fits a module behind them. With retrofit your switchboard looks the same, and the switches still work by hand. The how it works page shows it with pictures.

What your home needs

  • Wi-Fi and internet for control from the app. Your switches always work by hand without them.

  • Switchboxes with enough space for the modules.

  • Suitable wiring. Some modules need a wire called the neutral, which not every box has.

You do not need to check these yourself. A home survey does it, box by box.

Mistakes beginners make

  • Buying gadgets first. Look at your switchboxes before you buy anything.

  • Treating every appliance alike. A geyser needs a module built for heavy loads. A light module must not be used on it.

  • Doing mains wiring yourself. Use a trained electrician.

  • Believing every claim. Ask what works today and what is only planned.

  • Forgetting the family. Choose a setup that parents, children and guests can use without a phone.

Common questions

Is it safe? Fitted by trained electricians who follow a safety checklist, yes. If a wiring problem is found, you should be told before any work is done.

What if the internet stops? You use the switches by hand, as always. App control returns with the connection.

Can I talk to it? Voice control with Alexa or Google is planned for Homeasy and is not available yet.

What does it cost? It depends on your rooms and appliances. An exact price needs a survey. Our estimator helps you see which modules you would need.

Is there a warranty? Homeasy modules carry a 3-year warranty against manufacturing defects.

A simple plan

  1. List the three or four switches you most wish you could control from your phone.

  2. Have your switchboxes and Wi-Fi checked.

  3. Get a written quote for those rooms.

  4. Live with it for a while, then decide what to add.

That is the whole of home automation for beginners. When you are ready for step two, book a free home survey. The FAQ answers more questions in the meantime.
